title: Government Shutdown Market Impact: What Investors Need to Know
summary: Historical data shows the S&P 500 has averaged a 4.4% gain during government shutdowns since 1976, with GDP losses typically modest and temporary. The 2025 six-week shutdown — the longest on record — offers a detailed case study of market and economic effects.
body_markdown:
When Washington can't agree on a budget, markets pay attention — but the government shutdown market impact is often more nuanced than the headlines suggest. Based on data from every federal shutdown since 1976, the S&P 500 has historically shown resilience, gaining an average of 4.4% during these events. Understanding the mechanics, historical patterns, and sector-level dynamics can help investors make more informed decisions.


**Key Takeaways**


-


The S&P 500 has averaged a 4.4% gain during government shutdowns since 1976, though results vary widely by event.


-


GDP typically takes only a modest hit — roughly 0.05–0.2 percentage points per week — with much of the lost output recovered after funding resumes.


-


U.S. Treasury bonds have historically served as a safe-haven asset during shutdowns, with 10-year yields falling an average of 2.2 basis points.


-


The 2025 shutdown (Oct. 1–Nov. 12) lasted six weeks — the longest on record — and the CBO estimated a cumulative real GDP loss of $11 billion.


-


Defense and healthcare sectors have tended to outperform the broader market during shutdown periods, though results differ by event.


-


Investors who maintained consistent strategies through past shutdowns generally saw positive returns over the following 12 months.


---


## Part 1. How Government Shutdowns Work and Why They Happen


Understanding the mechanics behind a shutdown helps investors anticipate potential market effects and avoid overreacting to political noise.


### 1.1 The Annual Funding Cycle and Continuing Resolutions


Each year, Congress must pass 12 appropriations bills to fund federal agencies before September 30 — the end of the federal fiscal year. According to American Century Investments, the last time Congress successfully passed all required bills on time was in 1996.


When deadlines are missed, Congress often passes a **continuing resolution (CR)** — a temporary law that keeps funding flowing while negotiations continue. If neither a CR nor the appropriations bills pass by midnight on September 30, a government shutdown begins.


A government shutdown occurs when Congress fails to pass appropriations legislation or a continuing resolution, causing federal agencies to halt or scale back non-essential operations.


American Century Investments —[https://www.americancentury.com/insights/government-shutdown-market-impact/](https://www.americancentury.com/insights/government-shutdown-market-impact/)


### 1.2 What Shutdowns Actually Affect (and What They Don't)


Not every government function stops during a shutdown. In fiscal year 2024, discretionary spending — the portion directly affected — accounted for roughly 27% of the federal government's $6.8 trillion budget.


Mandatory programs like Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid continue uninterrupted because they're funded through separate long-term mechanisms. Essential services like postal delivery and interest payments on U.S. debt also continue. However, functions such as scientific research, passport processing, national park access, and food safety inspections may be paused or curtailed.


---


## Part 2. Government Shutdown Market Impact on Stocks: Historical Data


Equity markets tend to be more resilient during shutdowns than many investors expect. The data spanning nearly 50 years of shutdowns tells an instructive story.


### 2.1 S&P 500 Performance During and After Shutdowns


Stock performance during shutdowns has been mixed but generally positive. The S&P 500 has gained an average of 4.4% during government shutdowns and remained in positive territory during the last five shutdowns, according to Morgan Stanley research.


Returns during individual events vary significantly — ranging from a 3.9% decline during the October 1979 shutdown to a 9.3% gain during the 2018–2019 partial shutdown. More broadly, American Century's analysis shows that investors who stayed invested through past shutdowns generally saw gains over the following 12 months.


**Past performance does not guarantee future results.**


Morgan Stanley —[https://www.morganstanley.com/articles/government-shutdown-economic-impact-2025](https://www.morganstanley.com/articles/government-shutdown-economic-impact-2025)


During the 2025 shutdown, the S&P 500 actually rose to an all-time record high in the first week of the shutdown, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The 10-year Treasury yield edged down, and volatility measures across stocks, bonds, and currencies remained subdued despite ongoing political gridlock.


J.P. Morgan Asset Management —[https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/adv/insights/market-insights/market-updates/notes-on-the-week-ahead/the-investment-implications-of-the-government-shutdown/](https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/adv/insights/market-insights/market-updates/notes-on-the-week-ahead/the-investment-implications-of-the-government-shutdown/)


### 2.2 Sector Opportunities: Defense and Healthcare


During shutdowns since 1995, the defense sector has gained an average of 5.2% and the healthcare sector has advanced 2.3%, compared with the S&P 500's average 3% return over the same periods. However, sector-level performance is not uniform across every shutdown.


During the 2018–2019 partial shutdown, defense outperformed the S&P 500 while healthcare lagged. In the 2013 full shutdown, the pattern reversed — healthcare outperformed while defense lagged due to paused contracts and payments. Investors seeking sector-level exposure during a shutdown period should be aware of this variability and evaluate positions accordingly.


Morgan Stanley notes that, over the longer term, defense may potentially benefit from fiscal support, government prioritization, AI adoption, and geopolitical trends — though no near-term performance outcome can be guaranteed.


---


## Part 3. How a Government Shutdown Affects Treasury Bonds and Fixed Income


Beyond equities, the bond market also responds to shutdown dynamics — and the direction of that response has historically favored investors in U.S. Treasuries.


### 3.1 Bond Market Volatility During Shutdowns


Bond volatility during shutdowns is not a foregone conclusion. The MOVE Index — a measure of expected Treasury volatility — rose 3.6% during the 1990 shutdown and 7.2% during the 1995–1996 shutdown. But the same index fell 12.6% and 14.8% during the 2013 and 2018–2019 shutdowns, respectively.


This inconsistency underscores the importance of context. The state of the economy, the prevailing interest rate environment, and the duration of the shutdown all shape how bond markets respond. Investors should evaluate current conditions rather than assume a uniform historical pattern will hold.


### 3.2 Treasuries as a Safe-Haven Asset


On average, during shutdowns since 1976, the 10-year Treasury yield has fallen approximately 2.2 basis points while prices have edged higher — a signal that investors tend to seek safety in U.S. government bonds during periods of political uncertainty. Crucially, the U.S. government can still pay bondholders during a shutdown, so coupon payments on Treasuries are not at risk.


Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Office noted that, given the elevated yield environment in recent years, U.S. Treasuries remain relatively attractive and may offer a degree of resilience for investors concerned about shutdown-related volatility. That said, fixed-income investments carry interest rate risk and other risks that investors should review.


---


## Part 4. Government Shutdown GDP Impact: The 2025 Case Study


The 2025 government shutdown — which ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025 — offers the most detailed recent case study of a prolonged federal funding gap and its macroeconomic consequences.


### 4.1 Direct GDP Effects and Forecaster Estimates


The 2025 shutdown began at the start of FY2026 when Congress failed to pass appropriations bills or a continuing resolution by September 30. Funding was restored when P.L. 119-37 was signed into law on November 12, 2025, ending a six-week shutdown. All affected federal employees were paid retroactively.


The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the six-week shutdown would reduce annualized real GDP growth in Q4 2025 by approximately 1.5 percentage points, with a corresponding rebound of 2.2 percentage points expected in Q1 2026. By Q1 FY2027, the CBO projected the cumulative real GDP loss at $11 billion — less than 1% of GDP.


Congressional Research Service —[https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48832](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48832)


Goldman Sachs estimated the shutdown would reduce Q4 2025 annualized GDP growth by 1.15 percentage points, with a slightly larger boost of 1.3 percentage points expected in Q1 2026. EY-Parthenon estimated that through the first week of November, the shutdown had shaved approximately 0.8 percentage points off quarterly GDP growth, equivalent to roughly $55 billion in lost output.


The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee, in its December 2025 meeting minutes, expected the shutdown to reduce real GDP growth by approximately 1 percentage point in Q4 2025, with a corresponding boost in Q1 2026.


Federal Reserve Board of Governors —[https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20251210.htm](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20251210.htm)


### 4.2 Employment Impact


The 2025 shutdown furloughed an estimated 670,000 or more federal employees — roughly 0.4% of total nonfarm employment. An additional 730,000 "essential workers" continued working without pay during the shutdown period, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.


The Administration estimated that approximately 60,000 private sector jobs were also lost as a result of the shutdown. Federal contractor jobs were among the most directly exposed, as contractors — unlike federal employees — are not guaranteed back pay after a shutdown ends.


The Current Population Survey (used to calculate the unemployment rate) was not conducted in October 2025 due to the shutdown, meaning the official unemployment rate for that month remains unknown. This represented a significant gap in economic data availability.


### 4.3 Consumer Confidence and Indirect Effects


The 2025 shutdown also weighed on consumer and investor confidence. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell in both October and November 2025, with the November reading hitting its lowest level since 2022. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell notably in November 2025 to its lowest point since April.


Consumers cited the shutdown alongside other concerns — including inflation and trade policy — as factors weighing on their outlook. The U.S. Small Business Administration reported that the shutdown prevented the delivery of $5.3 billion in loans to approximately 10,000 small businesses. The U.S. Travel Association estimated the shutdown cost $1 billion per week to the travel economy.

**Understand Circuit Breakers and Trading Halts**


During periods of elevated market volatility — which can coincide with sharp political developments — exchanges may implement circuit breakers. These are mechanisms used by stock exchanges to halt trading during severe market declines, designed to prevent panic selling and allow time for investors to assess conditions. Levels are based on declines in the S&P 500 index.

## The Bottom Line


Government shutdowns generate significant political noise, but historical data suggests their direct market impact is often modest and temporary. The S&P 500 has averaged gains during shutdown periods, bonds have broadly held up, and GDP losses have tended to reverse after funding resumes. For long-term investors, maintaining a disciplined strategy — supported by reliable research tools and real-time data — may offer more value than attempting to time short-term political events.
